Diagrams

A visual language: the kinds of picture an agent draws in its replies, so the author reads at a glance what words would take a page to say. For each kind: what it shows, when it fits and when it does not, its parts, how it is drawn.

USEHand them to an agent

Paste this into a project's CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md: it is read at every start, so the agent draws its pictures this way without being told. The agents' guides hand these over too. To give one kind in a conversation, copy it with its Copy for an agent button.

01Sequence diagram: who talks to whom

The course of events: the parts of a system as columns, what they send each other as arrows, top to bottom in time order. A request, a failure, a retry or a fix reads in one look, and today beside proposed shows only the change.

Fits when

  • Parts pass something along: a person, a browser, a server, a database, a job, an outside service.
  • The order matters: a failure, a retry, a timeout, a race; what happens where, and after what.
  • A fix changes the course: a step added, an event dropped, a call moved. Today beside proposed.

Not when

  • One part alone, nothing passed between: its states are a state diagram, its decisions a flowchart, its look a screenshot.
  • The order does not matter, only where the parts run or how the data links: a container sketch or an entity-relationship diagram.
  • The times matter more than who: a timeline.
  • Too many at once: more than five participants or ten messages. Split it in two, or say it in a table.
  • A change the author sees on screen: screenshots before and after say it better.

How it is drawn

  1. Participants: one column each, a plain icon above a short name. A person, a laptop or browser, a server, a database cylinder, a clock for a cronjob, a page for another writer or a file, a cloud for an outside service, a warning triangle for an error tracker. The icons carry most of the reading; the names stay short.
  2. Lifelines: a dashed vertical line under each participant.
  3. Messages: arrows between lifelines, top to bottom in time order, each with a few words. A request blue, a failure or an error red, a success or an answer green, what stays the same grey. A note on a step sits on its arrow: 13:05 INSERT … SELECT, 403 plan limit.
  4. Today beside proposed (or before beside after, today beside made): two framed panels, tagged, the same participants in the same order, so only the change differs. The change is drawn, not described: an event crossed out, a step added, a participant greyed.
  5. Around it: a title line with the item's id and what it is, one line of context under it (where, how often), one line of proof under the panels.
  6. In the app's colours, and drawn for the width it is shown at: its words no smaller than the text around it.

Examples

In the author's words
  • Pictures that are clear to me; I'd like agents to make pictures of this kind in their messages: it makes them easier to understand. And especially the icons. (2026-10-13 15:29)
  • It makes sense to make one diagrams page, where we add diagrams, describe what they are, when they fit and when they do not: a visual language of sorts. This is a good example of a diagram for the course of events. (15:50)

# Sequence diagram: who talks to whom

The course of events: the parts of a system as columns, what they send each
other as arrows, top to bottom in time order. A request, a failure, a retry or
a fix reads in one look, and today beside proposed shows only the change.

![Its parts: participants with an icon above the name, dashed lifelines under them, messages as arrows top to bottom; blue a request, green a success, red a failure, grey what stays the same](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_parts.svg)

## Fits when

- **Parts pass something along:** a person, a browser, a server, a database,
  a job, an outside service.
- **The order matters:** a failure, a retry, a timeout, a race; what happens
  where, and after what.
- **A fix changes the course:** a step added, an event dropped, a call moved.
  Today beside proposed.

## Not when

- **One part alone,** nothing passed between: its states are a
  [state diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/state.md), its decisions a [flowchart](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/flowchart.md), its
  look a screenshot.
- **The order does not matter,** only where the parts run or how the data
  links: a [container sketch](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/containers.md) or an
  [entity-relationship diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/entities.md).
- **The times matter more than who:** a [timeline](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/timeline.md).
- **Too many at once:** more than five participants or ten messages. Split
  it in two, or say it in a table.
- **A change the author sees on screen:** screenshots before and after say it
  better.

## How it is drawn

1. **Participants:** one column each, a plain icon above a short name. A
   person, a laptop or browser, a server, a database cylinder, a clock for a
   cronjob, a page for another writer or a file, a cloud for an outside
   service, a warning triangle for an error tracker. The icons carry most of
   the reading; the names stay short.
2. **Lifelines:** a dashed vertical line under each participant.
3. **Messages:** arrows between lifelines, top to bottom in time order, each
   with a few words. A request blue, a failure or an error red, a success or
   an answer green, what stays the same grey. A note on a step sits on its
   arrow: `13:05 INSERT … SELECT`, `403 plan limit`.
4. **Today beside proposed** (or before beside after, today beside made): two
   framed panels, tagged, the same participants in the same order, so only
   the change differs. The change is drawn, not described: an event crossed
   out, a step added, a participant greyed.
5. **Around it:** a title line with the item's id and what it is, one line of
   context under it (where, how often), one line of proof under the panels.
6. **In the app's colours,** and drawn for the width it is shown at: its words
   no smaller than the text around it.

![S4, a plan limit: today the browser sends an error event to the tracker after the upgrade window; proposed, no event](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_plan_limit.svg)

## Examples

![U2, an upload retried: before, a passing 500 fails the export; after, the job waits and puts the file again, and the export is done](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_upload_retried.svg)

![D1, a deadlock in a cronjob retried inside the run: today an error event and the rows a run later; made, once more at once and no event](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_deadlock_retried.svg)

![D1, the same deadlock with no change proposed: the retry drawn as what would be done only if it grows](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_deadlock_not_now.svg)

![E7, the exporter's upload: today a failed upload is an error event; proposed, retried up to 3 times, the file arrives, no event](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_exporter_upload.svg)

![One upload through a render service: the browser gets a signed URL from the API through Cloudflare, puts the file straight to S3, asks for a render; the API queues it and answers 202; later SQS starts Lambda, which renders to S3 and marks the job done](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_banner_render.svg)

02One case: today beside fixed

One real request, its answer today beside its answer with the fix: the question on top, two framed panels under it, red for today and green for the fix. Big numbers and what works and what is missing follow, so the one case stands for the rest.

Fits when

  • One real request shows the gap: a question a help chat cannot answer, a call that fails, a search that finds nothing.
  • The fix is content or data, and its effect is the answer itself: a table, a value, a reply.
  • The author must decide what to do next: the case convinces, the lists say what else is open and what each costs.

Not when

  • The course of messages between parts changes, not the answer: a sequence diagram, today beside proposed.
  • Many parts at once, each with its state: a status dashboard.
  • A change on screen: two screenshots, before and after.

How it is drawn

  1. The question: quoted big in a soft blue box, where it was asked and when in grey beside it. The real words, not a summary.
  2. Today: a red frame, a red cross in a circle and "Today:" with why it fails; inside, the real answer as given and a red tag ("not_covered").
  3. With the fix: a green frame, a green tick and "With" and the fix; inside, the answer it would give and a green tag ("answered"). Values go in a small table, a line between rows.
  4. A verdict under each: in bold, red or green, what the panel shows; a line under it says where the real answer was seen, or in amber what is still to confirm.
  5. KPI cards: four big numbers for the whole, each a few words of what it counts; red or amber for a count that stands for a gap.
  6. Two lists: "Works" with green ticks; "Missing, by effort" with a pill per item, red for work to do (small, medium), amber for what waits on an answer (wait, check, decide). The item the case is about first, in bold.
  7. Ticks and crosses are drawn as paths, not typed as glyphs, so every font shows them alike.
In the author's words
  • Add all of them, only make them anonymous: nothing about the company or anything personal. (2026-10-14 23:56, of the visual-lang drafts)

# One case: today beside fixed

One real request, its answer today beside its answer with the fix: the
question on top, two framed panels under it, red for today and green for
the fix. Big numbers and what works and what is missing follow, so the one
case stands for the rest.

![A shop's help chat asked how much shipping to Canada is: today a vague reply, not covered; with a shipping-rates article, a table of four rates, answered; then the numbers, what works and what is missing, by effort](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/case_shipping.svg)

  [status dashboard](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/dashboard.md).
- **A change on screen:** two screenshots, before and after.

1. **The question:** quoted big in a soft blue box, where it was asked and
   when in grey beside it. The real words, not a summary.
2. **Today:** a red frame, a red cross in a circle and "Today:" with why it

3. **With the fix:** a green frame, a green tick and "With" and the fix;

4. **A verdict under each:** in bold, red or green, what the panel shows;
   a line under it says where the real answer was seen, or in amber what
   is still to confirm.
5. **KPI cards:** four big numbers for the whole, each a few words of what
   it counts; red or amber for a count that stands for a gap.
6. **Two lists:** "Works" with green ticks; "Missing, by effort" with a
   pill per item, red for work to do (small, medium), amber for what waits
   on an answer (wait, check, decide). The item the case is about first,

7. **Ticks and crosses** are drawn as paths, not typed as glyphs, so every

03State diagram: what moves a thing between its states

The states a thing has and what moves it from one to the next: a card's steps, a message's life, a job's run. Each state is a box; each arrow says what moves it.

Fits when

  • A thing has a few states, and the question is how it gets from one to another, or why it stays in one.
  • A state can be reached by more than one way, or left by a way that goes back.
  • A bug is a wrong state: stuck, skipped, or reached from where it should not be.

Not when

  • The order of calls between parts is the question: that is a sequence diagram.
  • One decision with its answers, no lasting state: a flowchart.
  • More than about eight states: draw the part that matters, and say the rest.

How it is drawn

  1. States: rounded boxes, a short name each. Coloured by what they mean: blue a step on the way, green the end that is wanted, orange one that needs a look.
  2. Transitions: the project's arrows, grey, each with the few words that move it (a click, an answer, a timeout).
  3. The start: a filled dot with an arrow into the first state.
  4. Around it: a title with the thing's name, one line of context, one line under it saying how to read it.
In the author's words
  • Add all five. (2026-10-13, as the note of 16:29 quotes it)
  • The new diagrams, I think, should go on the pages too, only in the same format as the other diagrams; and mind the arrows: take the ones the project uses. (16:33)

# State diagram: what moves a thing between its states

The states a thing has and what moves it from one to the next: a card's
steps, a message's life, a job's run. Each state is a box; each arrow says
what moves it.

![A sign-in card: from signed out through the code and the wait to saved; a refused code goes back for a new link, an unread token is shown in its window](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/state_sign_in.svg)

## Fits when

- **A thing has a few states,** and the question is how it gets from one to
  another, or why it stays in one.
- **A state can be reached by more than one way,** or left by a way that
  goes back.
- **A bug is a wrong state:** stuck, skipped, or reached from where it
  should not be.

## Not when

- **The order of calls between parts** is the question: that is a
  [sequence diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/sequence.md).
- **One decision with its answers,** no lasting state: a
  [flowchart](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/flowchart.md).
- **More than about eight states:** draw the part that matters, and say the
  rest.

## How it is drawn

1. **States:** rounded boxes, a short name each. Coloured by what they mean:
   blue a step on the way, green the end that is wanted, orange one that
   needs a look.
2. **Transitions:** the project's arrows, grey, each with the few words
   that move it (a click, an answer, a timeout).
3. **The start:** a filled dot with an arrow into the first state.
4. **Around it:** a title with the thing's name, one line of context, one
   line under it saying how to read it.

04Flowchart: what is decided where

The decisions one action goes through, in order: each question a diamond, each answer its own arrow, each outcome a box.

Fits when

  • One action branches: a click, a request or a job that does different things depending on what it finds.
  • The question is which way it went, and why: an outcome nobody expected.
  • A rule has cases, and every case must be seen at once.

Not when

  • A thing lives through states and comes back to them: a state diagram.
  • Several parts take turns: a sequence diagram.
  • More than about six questions: split it, or say it as a table of cases.

How it is drawn

  1. Steps: rectangles; the one that starts it darker.
  2. Questions: diamonds, a few words ending in a question mark, the words inside the diamond.
  3. Answers: the project's arrows, one per answer, each labelled (yes, no, or the value).
  4. Outcomes: boxes coloured by what they mean: green done, orange refused or spent, blue the way on.
  5. Left to right for the main way, down for the answers that leave it.
In the author's words
  • Add all five. (2026-10-13, as the note of 16:29 quotes it)
  • The new diagrams, I think, should go on the pages too, only in the same format as the other diagrams; and mind the arrows: take the ones the project uses. (16:33)

# Flowchart: what is decided where

The decisions one action goes through, in order: each question a diamond,
each answer its own arrow, each outcome a box.

![What Paste decides: a token, running, this link; each answer leads to its own outcome](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/flowchart_paste.svg)

## Fits when

- **One action branches:** a click, a request or a job that does different
  things depending on what it finds.
- **The question is which way it went,** and why: an outcome nobody
  expected.
- **A rule has cases,** and every case must be seen at once.

## Not when

- **A thing lives through states** and comes back to them: a
  [state diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/state.md).
- **Several parts take turns:** a [sequence diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/sequence.md).
- **More than about six questions:** split it, or say it as a table of
  cases.

## How it is drawn

1. **Steps:** rectangles; the one that starts it darker.
2. **Questions:** diamonds, a few words ending in a question mark, the
   words inside the diamond.
3. **Answers:** the project's arrows, one per answer, each labelled (yes,
   no, or the value).
4. **Outcomes:** boxes coloured by what they mean: green done, orange
   refused or spent, blue the way on.
5. **Left to right** for the main way, **down** for the answers that leave
   it.

05Known and open questions: how it works, and the gaps

How something works, stage by stage, with the facts read from the code and the questions no one can answer yet, each where it arises. A panel per stage, left to right; the questions inside the panel they belong to; a row of big numbers under them.

Fits when

  • Someone asks how a thing works, and part of the answer is "no one knows yet".
  • The facts and the gaps must be told apart: what the code says, beside what a person still has to decide or find out.
  • A meeting needs its questions: each one shown where it bites, not in a list at the end.

Not when

  • What is decided where, step by step: a flowchart.
  • A thing's states and what moves it between them: a state diagram.
  • Where many parts stand: a status dashboard.

How it is drawn

  1. The title says both halves: "how it works, and what we don't know", and the line under it says what green and amber mean.
  2. Stages: a green panel each, numbered "1 · Buying", left to right, an arrow between them; a few short lines of facts, the key figures in bold.
  3. Questions: an amber note inside the panel where the question arises, a thick amber bar on its left; the question in bold, and in grey what is known so far.
  4. Big numbers: a row under the panels, each a number and two lines of what it counts; amber or red when it stands for a gap.
  5. Facts only in green: a line in a green panel is read from the code or a log; a guess is a question, and goes in amber.
In the author's words
  • Add all of them, only make them anonymous: nothing about the company or anything personal. (2026-10-14 23:56, of the visual-lang drafts)

# Known and open questions: how it works, and the gaps

How something works, stage by stage, with the facts read from the code
and the questions no one can answer yet, each where it arises. A panel per
stage, left to right; the questions inside the panel they belong to; a row
of big numbers under them.

![Gift cards in a small shop: buying, spending and expiring as three green panels of facts; amber questions inside them, a refund, two orders at once, a return, a reminder, the law; 1 240 cards sold, 3 400 left unspent, 5 open questions, 0 reminders sent](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/questions_gift_cards.svg)

## Fits when

- **Someone asks how a thing works,** and part of the answer is "no one
  knows yet".
- **The facts and the gaps must be told apart:** what the code says,
  beside what a person still has to decide or find out.
- **A meeting needs its questions:** each one shown where it bites, not
  in a list at the end.

## Not when

- **What is decided where,** step by step: a
  [flowchart](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/flowchart.md).
- **A thing's states** and what moves it between them: a
  [state diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/state.md).
- **Where many parts stand:** a [status dashboard](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/dashboard.md).

## How it is drawn

1. **The title says both halves:** "how it works, and what we don't
   know", and the line under it says what green and amber mean.
2. **Stages:** a green panel each, numbered "1 · Buying", left to right,
   an arrow between them; a few short lines of facts, the key figures in
   bold.
3. **Questions:** an amber note inside the panel where the question
   arises, a thick amber bar on its left; the question in bold, and in
   grey what is known so far.
4. **Big numbers:** a row under the panels, each a number and two lines
   of what it counts; amber or red when it stands for a gap.
5. **Facts only in green:** a line in a green panel is read from the
   code or a log; a guess is a question, and goes in amber.

06Timeline: what happened when

Events at their moments, from a log: one line of time, left to right, each event a dot with its time and a few words.

Fits when

  • A log tells it: times matter, and the gaps between them.
  • The question is what came before what, or what happened while something else waited.
  • One event went wrong among others that did not.

Not when

  • Who sent what to whom matters more than when: a sequence diagram.
  • The times do not matter, only the order of states: a state diagram.
  • Hundreds of events: pick the few that tell it, and say how many were left out.

How it is drawn

  1. The line of time: one grey line, left to right.
  2. Events: a dot on the line, a stem to its label, the time in bold above a few words. The labels go above and below in turn, so close events do not collide.
  3. Colours: blue for what went as it should, green for an end that is wanted, red for what went wrong.
  4. What went wrong gets a note of its own, in red, under its event.

# Timeline: what happened when

Events at their moments, from a log: one line of time, left to right, each
event a dot with its time and a few words.

![A sign-in second by second: started, link opened, code typed, ended with the token unread, then Paste starting a new sign-in](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/timeline_sign_in.svg)

## Fits when

- **A log tells it:** times matter, and the gaps between them.
- **The question is what came before what,** or what happened while
  something else waited.
- **One event went wrong** among others that did not.

## Not when

- **Who sent what to whom** matters more than when: a
  [sequence diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/sequence.md).
- **The times do not matter,** only the order of states: a
  [state diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/state.md).
- **Hundreds of events:** pick the few that tell it, and say how many were
  left out.

## How it is drawn

1. **The line of time:** one grey line, left to right.

09Entity-relationship: what data there is and how it links

The kinds of data a system keeps, their main fields, and how many of one go with one of another: 1 to n, n to n, marked on each line's ends.

Fits when

  • The question is about data: where something is kept, what points to what.
  • A change touches a link: one becomes many, or a link goes away.
  • A newcomer reads the storage before the code.

Not when

  • Where the data lives (which machine, which service): a container sketch.
  • What happens to one record over time: a state diagram.
  • Every field of every table: keep the main ones; the schema is in the code.

How it is drawn

  1. Entities: a box per kind of data, its name in bold on a tinted band, its main fields under it.
  2. Links: plain lines, no arrowheads, a verb under the line (holds, has, linked in).
  3. Their ends, crow's feet: two short bars across the line where it is one, a three-pronged foot with a bar before it where it is many (one or more). 1 and n in bold beside them, for a reader who does not know the marks.
  4. Left to right in the order a reader meets them; a child under its parent.

# Entity-relationship: what data there is and how it links

The kinds of data a system keeps, their main fields, and how many of one go
with one of another: 1 to n, n to n, marked on each line's ends.

![A note's data: a note holds messages, messages are linked in subjects, a message has files](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/entities_notes.svg)

## Fits when

- **The question is about data:** where something is kept, what points to
  what.
- **A change touches a link:** one becomes many, or a link goes away.
- **A newcomer reads the storage** before the code.

## Not when

- **Where the data lives** (which machine, which service): a
  [container sketch](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/containers.md).
- **What happens to one record over time:** a [state diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/state.md).
- **Every field of every table:** keep the main ones; the schema is in the
  code.

## How it is drawn

1. **Entities:** a box per kind of data, its name in bold on a tinted band,
   its main fields under it.
2. **Links:** plain lines, no arrowheads, a verb under the line (holds, has,
   linked in).
3. **Their ends, crow's feet:** two short bars across the line where it is
   one, a three-pronged foot with a bar before it where it is many (one or
   more). **1** and **n** in bold beside them, for a reader who does not
   know the marks.
4. **Left to right** in the order a reader meets them; a child under its
   parent.

10Status dashboard: where each part stands

A RAG status dashboard (red, amber, green): the state of many parts at once, each a tile coloured by its state. Big numbers on top, the tiles grouped below, the gaps gathered at the end. Two more kinds at the end: tiles coloured by where each part is, and a whole beside its gap.

Fits when

  • The question is where things stand: many parts, each in place, stale or missing.
  • The reader must find the gaps fast: a project's checks, a release, an audit of what is covered.
  • The same view is read again later, and the colours show what moved.

Not when

  • One thing and its states over time: a state diagram.
  • What happened in what order: a timeline or a sequence diagram.
  • A few parts only: a sentence or a list says it; a dashboard needs enough tiles to scan.

How it is drawn

  1. The key: green in place and checked, amber stale or unchecked, red missing or failed, in one line under the title.
  2. KPI cards: three or four big numbers on top, each a word of what it counts and a line of context, coloured like the worst it stands for.
  3. The status board: a panel per area, its name and a line of what it holds; a tile per part, its name in bold and its state in its colour.
  4. The gaps: the amber and red tiles again, gathered in a panel at the end, so the reader does not hunt for them.
  5. Real states only: a tile's word says why it has its colour ("1 failed", "no test"), never just "bad".

Coloured by where it is

When the question is where each part is, not how it is, the colours name places: production, development, the working tree. The list behind a tile opens on a click, in a panel beside the grid.

  1. A card per place, in the colour its tiles get: green, on production as it is; blue, on development and not released; amber, only in the working tree and not committed.
  2. Each tile in the colour of its latest change: its name in bold, a small word for what is not out yet ("not released").
  3. A red dot on a tile: a question it cannot answer, its data missing.
  4. The key under the grid, the red dot in it too.
  5. Details on a click: the chosen tile gets a dark outline; the panel beside the grid shows its name, a tag of where it is, and short sections, headed in small caps, of a few bullets each. The tile never grows to hold its list.

A whole and its gap

When the question is how much is covered, one bar shows the whole and what is missing from it; a row of squares counts the runs.

  • The bar: a segment per kind, as wide as its count, dark green, light green, a thin strip for the rest.
  • The gap: a dashed red segment at the end, hatched soft red, its label on a pill: "+ coupons, sizes".
  • A grey line under the bar names the strip and the dashed part.
  • Units as squares, in rows: filled green passed, filled red failed, empty with a red outline skipped. A grey line under them says which failed, when, and why the rest were skipped.
In the author's words
  • Let's add it to the diagrams too, but first make a few sketches. (2026-10-14 13:45, of a status dashboard)
  • Sketch: A, the full dashboard. (13:49)
  • Add all of them, only make them anonymous: nothing about the company or anything personal. (2026-10-14 23:56, of the visual-lang drafts)

11Versions: which version runs where

A table of what is deployed: one row per part, its version, its commit and its date, and whether it is the latest. A verdict in a sentence on top, what "latest" means at the bottom.

Fits when

  • The question is what runs now: before a release, after an incident, when a fix should already be live.
  • Some parts are deployed by hand, and the reader must see which of them no one can vouch for.
  • Many parts, each with its own version, too many to keep in mind.

Not when

  • How the parts talk to each other: a containers diagram.
  • Where the parts run: a cloud diagram.
  • How healthy they are now: a service map or a status dashboard.

How it is drawn

  1. The time it was read, under the title: a version table is true only for the moment it was taken.
  2. The verdict first: one sentence, its first half in bold, says what the table shows before the reader reads a row.
  3. A row per deployed part: its name in bold, the version big and bold, the commit in the look of a link, the date.
  4. Latest or not: a green tick and "latest", or an amber "? unknown"; never a guess. A grey note says why: "nothing on main is left out", or how it was deployed and the newest code there is.
  5. What "latest" means, in a line under the table, and where it was read from.
  6. The reader on top, agents below: the summary first; the sources of every version, the files and logs it was read from, go under a line, in a part of their own for agents.

  3. Paths: the main one bold blue, the background one dashed green, the rest thin grey; a key under the drawing.

# Layered diagram: the tiers a request passes

The parts in columns by tier, left to right in the order a request meets
them: the edge, the entry, the compute, the background work, the data.
The main path bold, the side paths in their own style.

![The render service in five tiers: Cloudflare at the edge, the load balancer and nginx at the entry, the API in compute, SQS and Lambda for background work, PostgreSQL, Redis and S3 as data; the main path blue, the render jobs dashed green](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/tiers_banners.svg)

## Fits when

- **How deep a request goes:** which tiers it crosses before an answer.
- **Where a part belongs:** a new service placed in its tier, or one in
  the wrong one.
- **A caching or scaling talk:** what each tier absorbs.

## Not when

- **Where things run, in which network:** a
  [cloud architecture diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/cloud.md).
- **Many links between many parts:** a [dependency matrix](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/matrix.md).

## How it is drawn

1. **Tiers:** columns with a name and a line under it, left to right.
2. **Parts:** boxes in their tier; outside parties outside the columns.
3. **Paths:** the main one bold blue, the background one dashed green, the
   rest thin grey; a key under the drawing.

15Isometric diagram: the system as a model

The same parts as blocks on an isometric floor, the networks as raised platforms, the main paths along the grid: a picture to point at on a slide, read before any word.

Fits when

  • A slide or a talk: the whole system at once, for people who will not read a diagram's notation.
  • Groups matter more than links: what sits together on which platform.

Not when

  • Exact links, ports or order: any other kind says it better; an isometric picture hides lines behind blocks.
  • The picture will change often: the layout is slow to redraw.

How it is drawn

  1. The floor: a faint isometric grid; places as dashed outlines on it.
  2. Platforms: a raised slab per network, its name on a pill.
  3. Parts: blocks for services, cylinders for stores, a name on a pill.
  4. Paths: only the main ones, along the grid, coloured by kind.
In the author's words
  • I am more interested in the topology of computer systems: some complex architecture with queues, Cloudflare, S3, Lambda, proxies, load balancers, databases, all of that. (2026-10-14 18:13)
  • Let us add these pictures to the documentation. Which get used is not clear yet, but let them be; we will see. (19:01)

16Service map: what talks to what, live

What a tracing tool draws from real traffic: each service a circle with a ring for its health, each link as thick as its traffic, the numbers on the links. The unwell one stands out at a glance.

Fits when

  • On call: which hop is slow or failing, and who depends on it.
  • Traffic matters: where the requests go, how many.
  • The real system, as measured, not as designed.

Not when

  • The design, before it runs: a C4 container diagram.
  • How much of the traffic stops where: a Sankey diagram.

How it is drawn

  1. Services: circles laid out freely, an icon inside, the name and one number under it.
  2. Health: the ring green, orange when slow, red when failing, dashed grey for what is not traced.
  3. Links: thickness by traffic, "N req/s" on a pill; a legend.

- **How much of the traffic stops where:** a [Sankey diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/sankey.md).

## How it is drawn

1. **Services:** circles laid out freely, an icon inside, the name and one
   number under it.
2. **Health:** the ring green, orange when slow, red when failing, dashed
   grey for what is not traced.
3. **Links:** thickness by traffic, "N req/s" on a pill; a legend.

17Sankey diagram: where the traffic goes, how much

Traffic as bands that split and end, each as wide as its share: what a cache absorbs, what reaches each part behind it.

Fits when

  • Capacity and cost: how much each layer absorbs and passes on.
  • A cache's worth: the share that never reaches the origin.

Not when

  • Who calls whom: a service map or a layered diagram.
  • Flows too small to see beside big ones: say them in a line under it.

How it is drawn

  1. Columns: a thin bar per part, its name above.
  2. Bands: from bar to bar, widths to one scale, each with its number.
  3. Ends: what stops early ends at its own bar, in its own colour.

Traffic as bands that split and end, each as wide as its share: what a
cache absorbs, what reaches each part behind it.

## Fits when

## Not when

- **Who calls whom:** a [service map](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/servicemap.md) or a
  [layered diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/tiers.md).
- **Flows too small to see** beside big ones: say them in a line under it.

## How it is drawn

1. **Columns:** a thin bar per part, its name above.
2. **Bands:** from bar to bar, widths to one scale, each with its number.

18Data flow diagram: where data crosses a trust boundary

The threat modeller's view: outside parties, processes and data stores, the flows between them labelled with the data they carry, and the trust boundaries as red dashed lines. Each crossing gets a number to discuss.

Fits when

  • A security review or a threat model: each crossing is a place to ask what can go wrong (STRIDE per crossing).
  • Privacy: where personal data goes and what leaves.

Not when

  • Ports and rules: a network diagram.
  • The order of one request: a sequence diagram.

How it is drawn

  1. Notation: outside parties as boxes, processes as circles, stores as two open lines; a key.
  2. Flows: arrows named by their data ("card token"), not by protocol.
  3. Boundaries: red dashed lines; a numbered badge where a flow crosses one, the risky ones noted under the drawing.

- **The order of one request:** a [sequence diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/sequence.md).

## How it is drawn

1. **Notation:** outside parties as boxes, processes as circles, stores as
   two open lines; a key.
2. **Flows:** arrows named by their data ("card token"), not by protocol.
3. **Boundaries:** red dashed lines; a numbered badge where a flow
   crosses one, the risky ones noted under the drawing.

19Dependency matrix: every link in a grid

The parts as rows and the same parts as columns; a filled cell where the row calls the column. Every link at once, however many, with no lines to cross.

Fits when

  • Many parts: where a graph turns into a hairball.
  • Layers and cycles: with the parts in order, a call below the diagonal goes against the layers.

Not when

  • A few parts: a layered diagram reads faster.
  • The order of the calls: a sequence diagram.

How it is drawn

  1. Rows and columns: the same parts in the same order, the column names turned upright, groups bracketed on the left.
  2. Cells: filled where the row calls the column, with a port or a verb when it fits.
  3. Reading: a line under it says how ("the row calls the column").

# Dependency matrix: every link in a grid

The parts as rows and the same parts as columns; a filled cell where the
row calls the column. Every link at once, however many, with no lines to
cross.

![Twelve parts of the render service in a grid: users call Cloudflare on 443, the API calls Redis, PostgreSQL, the replica, SQS and Stripe; the one call below the diagonal, Lambda writing back to PostgreSQL, in orange](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/matrix_banners.svg)

## Fits when

- **Many parts:** where a graph turns into a hairball.
- **Layers and cycles:** with the parts in order, a call below the
  diagonal goes against the layers.

## Not when

- **A few parts:** a [layered diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/tiers.md) reads faster.
- **The order of the calls:** a [sequence diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/sequence.md).

## How it is drawn

1. **Rows and columns:** the same parts in the same order, the column
   names turned upright, groups bracketed on the left.
2. **Cells:** filled where the row calls the column, with a port or a verb
   when it fits.
3. **Reading:** a line under it says how ("the row calls the column").

20Call graph: which function calls which

A program from its entry down: each function a box, an arrow to each one it calls, the related ones framed together, the helpers everything leans on at the bottom.

Fits when

  • A change is planned: what calls the function, what it touches.
  • A newcomer reads a script: its steps and its shared helpers.
  • Dead code: a function nothing points at.

Not when

  • Files, not functions: a module graph.
  • What the script reads and writes: a data flow of a script.
  • Where the time goes: a flame graph.

How it is drawn

  1. Layers: the entry at the top, each call one row lower.
  2. Groups: light frames for the functions of one step.
  3. Too many: the main ones drawn, the rest a "+N more" box.

21Data flow of a script: files in, steps, files out

What a script reads on the left, the steps it makes of it in the middle, what it writes on the right; each arrow named by what passes along it.

Fits when

  • "Where does my edit end up?": from a source file to the page.
  • A build, an import, an export: a script whose job is files.

Not when

  • The functions inside: a call graph.
  • A system of services: a layered diagram.

How it is drawn

  1. Files: a page icon and the path; inputs left, outputs right, the ones rewritten in place in their own colour.
  2. Steps: rounded boxes in the middle.
  3. Arrows: named by what passes ("Markdown", "index", "HTML").

22Module graph: which file needs which

The files of a project as boxes in their folders, an arrow from each file to each one it requires, the packages from outside in their own shape.

Fits when

  • What breaks when a file changes: everything that points at it.
  • Cycles and layers: an arrow that goes back up.
  • What a script drags in from outside.

Not when

  • Functions inside one file: a call graph.
  • Hundreds of files: a dependency matrix.

How it is drawn

  1. Folders: dashed frames named at the top left.
  2. Files and packages: a box with a folded corner for a file, a rounded one with a cube for a package.
  3. Arrows: blue for a require, dashed orange for running it as a process; "+N more" for the rest.

23Flame graph: where one run spends its time

One measured run: each call stack a column of bars, the caller under the callee, each bar as wide as its share of the time. The widest bars at the top are where the time goes.

Fits when

  • "Why is it slow?": the time of a run by function, measured.
  • Before and after a speed fix: the same bar, narrower.

Not when

  • The structure, not the time: a call graph.
  • Time across services: a sequence diagram of a trace.

How it is drawn

  1. Bars: bottom-up, the whole run at the bottom, widths to one scale, the name and the milliseconds in each.
  2. Too narrow: a letter in the bar, its name in a key; a narrow part that matters zoomed above.
  3. Self time: the bars that spend it themselves marked in orange.

# Flame graph: where one run spends its time

One measured run: each call stack a column of bars, the caller under the
callee, each bar as wide as its share of the time. The widest bars at the
top are where the time goes.

![One run of bin/build, 1531 ms: 889 ms waiting for bin/self-check, 363 ms in build_index_html, most of that reading whole images only to learn their size](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/flame_build.svg)

## Fits when

- **"Why is it slow?":** the time of a run by function, measured.
- **Before and after a speed fix:** the same bar, narrower.

## Not when

- **The structure, not the time:** a [call graph](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/callgraph.md).
- **Time across services:** a [sequence diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/sequence.md) of a trace.

## How it is drawn

1. **Bars:** bottom-up, the whole run at the bottom, widths to one scale,
   the name and the milliseconds in each.
2. **Too narrow:** a letter in the bar, its name in a key; a narrow part
   that matters zoomed above.
3. **Self time:** the bars that spend it themselves marked in orange.

24Code map: how big each part is

A treemap of the code: each function a rectangle, its area its lines, grouped by the part of the program it belongs to.

Fits when

  • Where the code is: the big parts to split, the parts that grow.
  • A first look at a large file or project.

Not when

  • Who calls whom: a call graph.
  • Where the time goes: a flame graph; size is not cost.

How it is drawn

  1. Groups: a frame per part, its name and its lines in the header.
  2. Rectangles: one per function, area by lines, the name and the count when they fit.
  3. The small ones: merged into a dashed "N small functions" box.
